title: Chapter 1 — That Equality Naturally Gives Men A Taste For Free Institutions
paragraphs: I would fulfill the purpose of this book only imperfectly if, after having shown what opinions and sentiments the principle of equality suggests, I did not point out, before concluding, the general influence these same opinions and sentiments may have on the government of human societies. To succeed in this, I will often have to retrace my steps. But I trust the reader will not refuse to follow me along paths already known to him, which may lead to some new truth.

The principle of equality, which makes men independent of one another, gives them a habit and a taste for following, in their private actions, no guide but their own will. This complete independence, which they constantly enjoy toward their equals and in the course of private life, tends to make them look on all authority with a jealous eye, and quickly suggests to them the notion and the love of political freedom. Men living in such times have a natural bias toward free institutions. Take any one of them at random and search, if you can, his deepest instincts: you will find that of all governments, the one he will most readily conceive and most highly value is that whose head he has himself elected, and whose administration he can control. Of all the political effects produced by the equality of conditions, this love of independence is the first to strike the observer and to alarm the timid. It cannot be said that their alarm is entirely misplaced, for anarchy has a more formidable look in democratic countries than elsewhere. Since the citizens have no direct influence on each other, as soon as the supreme power of the nation fails—the power that kept them all in their several stations—it would seem that disorder must instantly reach its peak, and that, every man drawing aside in a different direction, the fabric of society must at once crumble away.

I am, however, persuaded that anarchy is not the principal evil democratic ages have to fear, but the least. For the principle of equality produces two tendencies: one leads men straight to independence, and may suddenly drive them into anarchy; the other leads them by a longer, more secret, but more certain road to servitude. Nations readily discern the first tendency, and are prepared to resist it; they are led away by the second without seeing where it is going. Hence it is especially important to point it out. For my own part, far from reproaching the principle of equality for making men unmanageable, it is this very feature that chiefly wins my approval. I admire the way it deposits in the mind and heart of man the dim conception and instinctive love of political independence, thus preparing the remedy for the evil it engenders. It is for this very reason that I am attached to it.
